name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,867

entries.clue: Teacher made knots in his hair (12)

indicators.note: Hair in knots has lost the order it was combed into, and letters left that way can be written out in any sequence.
Something put in a thing sits among its letters, so the tangled piece is planted inside the word beside it rather than added on the end.

blocks.note: a tress is a length of hair, and with HIS in front the eight letters split open after the first
the four letters of MADE, tangled into a new order

annotation.walkthrough: The surface sells a scruffy schoolmaster and the answer is a woman: 'his' belongs to the wordplay only, and never to the person being defined.
annotation.definitionFit: Teacher -> HEADMISTRESS: the woman in charge of a school is a teacher, the most senior one in the building, so the definition names her by her job.

entries.clue: Meaningful picture from reading out Mog's letters (5)

indicators.note: Reading something out means saying it rather than writing it, so what counts is the noise the characters make in the mouth.

blocks.note: the name is spelled M, O, G, and each of those three letters has a spoken name of its own

annotation.walkthrough: Say the three letter-names one after another and they run together into a word borrowed from Japanese, where it means picture-character.
annotation.definitionFit: Meaningful picture -> EMOJI: a tiny symbol typed in place of words, so the picture is doing the carrying that a sentence would otherwise do.

entries.clue: Tear up unfashionable husband's old cotton belt? (4,5)

indicators.note: A down entry is read bottom to top, so up tells you the word just clued is written into the grid the other way round.

blocks.note: to tear along a road is to speed, and those five letters go in backwards
what is out is no longer in fashion
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a form

annotation.walkthrough: 'Tear' is the verb that rhymes with air, not the one that comes with crying. The Cotton Belt is the old plantation country of the southern United States.
annotation.definitionFit: old cotton belt -> DEEP SOUTH: the states where cotton plantations once ruled the economy, Mississippi and Alabama among them, are still called the Deep South.

entries.clue: Faces court released to the public (6)

blocks.note: a defendant who faces something is up against it, and the passive phrase that says so needs this two-letter verb to stand it up
to take someone to court is to sue them, so the person in the dock has been sued

annotation.walkthrough: The whole trick is where the space goes: IS SUED, two words about a courtroom, run together into one word with no law in it at all.
annotation.definitionFit: released to the public -> ISSUED: a statement, a stamp or a passport that has been issued has been put out officially for anyone to have.

entries.clue: Grip case with empty travelator ahead (8)

indicators.note: Emptying a word tips out everything between its first and last letters, leaving just the two standing at the ends.
What is ahead goes first, so the pair just taken opens the answer instead of trailing along behind.

blocks.note: the moving walkway keeps only the letter it starts with and the letter it ends with
an action is a case brought before a court of law

annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' sits next to a travelator and looks like luggage at an airport. It is the legal sort, and the airport never comes into it.
annotation.definitionFit: Grip -> TRACTION: traction is the grip a tyre or a boot keeps on the ground, the friction that stops the thing sliding away.

entries.clue: Message from girl I am excited about (5)

indicators.note: Taking something from a phrase means lifting it out of what is already written there, one consecutive letter after another.
About means turned round, the way a ship comes about, so the run of letters is read the other way along the entry.

blocks.note: five letters in a row, starting in the middle of the first word and stopping just inside the last, read backwards

annotation.walkthrough: The girl is never named and 'I am' is not fodder to be shuffled. Every letter is already sitting in the clue, running the wrong way.
annotation.definitionFit: Message -> EMAIL: an email is a message sent electronically, so the definition is the general word standing in for one particular kind.

entries.clue: Severe wife burning trousers (9)

indicators.note: To trouser something is to pocket it, slipping it out of sight inside, so the letter beside this word goes within the other.

blocks.note: singeing is burning at the edges, and the word opens up after its first letter
W is the usual abbreviation for wife

annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' is a verb, British slang for quietly pocketing something, and that is the only word telling you one letter goes inside another.
annotation.definitionFit: Severe -> SWINGEING: swingeing cuts or fines are punishingly harsh ones, a British adjective with no connection at all to swinging.

entries.clue: Play guitar supporting Prince, an old 21 (5,1,6)

indicators.note: A support sits under what it holds up, and in a down entry underneath means later, so the guitar work goes below the royal name.

blocks.note: the younger of the two British princes born to Charles and Diana
to strum is to play a guitar by sweeping a hand across the strings
the article goes in as the two letters it is spelled with

annotation.walkthrough: A bare number sends you to that clue for the definition, so solve 21 across first. The middle initial stands for nothing: his parents could not choose between two grandfathers.
annotation.definitionFit: old 21 -> HARRY S TRUMAN: 21 across is the acronym for the American president, and Truman held that office from 1945, so he is a past one.

entries.clue: Practising lawyers troubling to Morse (7)

indicators.note: Something troubling will not let things settle, and letters that cannot settle finish up in an order nobody gave them.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

annotation.walkthrough: Morse is the Oxford detective of the television series, and the surface wants you reading him as a code. He is seven letters and a preposition.
annotation.definitionFit: Practising lawyers -> MOOTERS: a moot is the mock case law students argue for training, so mooters practise in the rehearsing sense, not the professional one.

entries.clue: 8's scheme for regenerating height with everyone in chocolate factory shrunk? (8,4)

indicators.note: One thing put in another sits between its parts, so the two short pieces named before this word are buried between the two named after.
A word that has shrunk has come up short, and what it loses is the letter standing at its end.

blocks.note: a Mars is a chocolate bar sold in every British newsagent
H is the standard abbreviation for height
all means everyone, every last one of them
a factory is a plant, and it comes up one letter short of that

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is selling Roald Dahl. The wordplay wants a confectionery brand and an industrial plant instead, and only the brand survives whole.
annotation.definitionFit: 8's scheme for regenerating -> MARSHALL PLAN: the American programme, named for Truman's secretary of state, that funded the rebuilding of western Europe after 1945.

entries.clue: Bad mushroom trip's beginning in a frenzy (7)

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, so a single character of the noun in front of this is all that is wanted.
One letter put in a phrase finishes up inside it, so the character just taken is planted within the words that follow.

blocks.note: a frenzy is a mania, with the article riding in front; the six letters split before the last one
trip hands over its opening letter and nothing else

annotation.walkthrough: A bad mushroom trip is the picture, and mushrooms really are the subject. This genus holds the death cap and the destroying angel.
annotation.definitionFit: Bad mushroom -> AMANITA: the amanitas are the toadstool genus that includes the death cap, so 'bad' means deadly poisonous rather than merely off.

entries.clue: Vet again checks animal that's caught cold (9)

indicators.note: Whatever is caught is held fast inside the thing that caught it, so the letter named after this word sits within the animal.

blocks.note: reins are what check a horse, and to rein in is to check
a pet is the animal kept at home, and its three letters open up after two
C is the letter on the cold tap

annotation.walkthrough: 'Vet' is the verb — to examine something closely before approving it — and not the animal doctor the pet in the wordplay keeps hinting at.
annotation.definitionFit: Vet again -> REINSPECT: to vet is to examine critically before giving approval, and the re- prefix asks for that examination a second time.

entries.clue: Cheap fizz from Majestic brought round (5)

indicators.note: Bringing a thing round turns it to face the other way, so the word beside this one is entered right to left.

blocks.note: majestic means regal, and those five letters are turned round

annotation.walkthrough: Majestic is a British wine chain, which is what makes the surface read as a shopping trip. The wordplay wants the adjective regal, spelled backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheap fizz -> LAGER: the pale gassy beer that is the cheapest pint in most bars, so both halves of the phrase point at it.

entries.clue: Hampshire's opener exploited fault as much as bowler could bear? (6)

definitions.text: as much as bowler could bear?

indicators.note: In cricket the opener is the batsman who goes in first, and a word's opener is likewise the letter it starts with.
A fault that is exploited gets worked at until it breaks open, and letters treated that way do not stay in the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: the county's name gives up its first letter and nothing more
the five letters of FAULT, shaken into another arrangement

annotation.walkthrough: Every word points at cricket: Hampshire, an English county side, its opening batsman, and a bowler taking wickets. The answer is about millinery.
annotation.definitionFit: as much as bowler could bear? -> HATFUL: a bowler is a hard round hat, so what one could hold is a hatful, the loose measure the word names.

entries.clue: B&B owner might stand round here (5,4)

definitions.text: B&B owner might stand round here

blocks.note: The surface has a landlord standing a round of drinks for his guests, which is the wrong sort of bar altogether.
A round is one slice off a loaf, and 'stand' is literal: at a bed-and-breakfast table the browned slices are stood upright in a wire frame.

annotation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay to hunt for — the sentence simply means the object twice over. British breakfast tables stand the slices up so they cool and stay crisp.
annotation.definitionFit: B&B owner might stand round here -> TOAST RACK: a round is a slice of bread, and the wire frame on a breakfast table is where the slices stand.

entries.clue: Offer suit to sell back, keeping current winter clothing (8)

indicators.note: In an across entry the way back is right to left, so the word before this one is written into the grid in reverse.
What you keep you hold on to and enclose, so the letter after this word is kept within the one already turned round.

blocks.note: to pay suit to somebody is to woo them, the old sense of courting
the four letters go in the other way round, and they open up before the last of them
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current

annotation.walkthrough: 'Offer suit' is the courtship sense rather than a tailor's, and 'current' is the electrical one. Two everyday words, both doing crossword jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: winter clothing -> WOOLLIES: woollies are the jumpers and socks knitted from wool that people pull on once the weather turns cold.

entries.clue: Title holder's fallen during road race at the start (9)

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so the fallen word drops in among the letters of the road.
The start of a word is the character it opens with, so the race gives up one letter and keeps the rest to itself.

blocks.note: a lane is a narrow road, and its four letters split after the third
race supplies its opening letter alone
someone fallen is down, and the word goes in whole

annotation.walkthrough: 'Title holder' sounds like a champion defending a belt. The title meant is the deed that proves who owns a piece of ground.
annotation.definitionFit: Title holder -> LANDOWNER: title is the legal term for ownership of property, so whoever holds the title to a field is the person who owns it.

entries.clue: Platonic relationship troubled Macron, in bed mostly (8)

indicators.note: A troubled thing is unsettled, and letters that will not settle can be set down in any order at all.
One word put in another sits between its letters, so the shuffled name lands inside the shortened word rather than beside it.
Mostly means all but a little, and the little left off the end of a word is its final letter.

blocks.note: bed drops its last letter, and the two that remain part company to take something in
the six letters of the French president's surname, rearranged

annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a headline about Macron's private life. The word itself is a portmanteau, brother spliced onto romance, coined for friendships between men.
annotation.definitionFit: Platonic relationship -> BROMANCE: a bromance is a close and affectionate friendship between two men with nothing sexual in it, which is what platonic means.

entries.clue: Biking kit verges on lingerie where she lives (8)

definitions.note: Kit is a mass noun for gear in general while the answer is plural, which is how motorcyclists talk: the jacket and the trousers are named together.

indicators.note: A verge is the strip at the edge of a road, so what is wanted is the letters standing at the two edges of the word after it.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the garment, with everything between them dropped
if something is at hers, it is where she lives, and the two words run together

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all underwear and roadside verges, and neither survives the parse: 'verges on' is an instruction rather than a description.
annotation.definitionFit: Biking kit -> LEATHERS: leathers are the thick hide jacket and trousers a motorcyclist wears as armour against the road.

entries.clue: Ass kept hidden in apprehension, age-related (6)

indicators.note: Something kept hidden inside a phrase has been there all along, written out in order, waiting for somebody to notice it.

blocks.note: six letters in a row, running across the comma and the hyphen, from the tail of one word to the middle of the next

annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface is about animals, so there is no reason to suspect a species lying across three words of a sentence about worry.
annotation.definitionFit: Ass -> ONAGER: definition by example, since the onager is one particular wild ass, the Asiatic species, rather than the animal in general.

entries.clue: Spice in fruitcake Margaret reduced (6)

indicators.note: Reducing a name here means using the short form its owner answers to, not chopping letters off the end of it.

blocks.note: a fruitcake is a nut in the slang sense, somebody crazy
the short form a Margaret goes by

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on the same move away from the kitchen: the fruitcake is a person rather than a cake, and Margaret is here only to be shortened.
annotation.definitionFit: Spice -> NUTMEG: the hard aromatic seed grated over custards and into mulled wine, one of the standard jars on a kitchen shelf.

entries.clue: Premier turned up to speak, missing point? (5)

indicators.note: Milk that has turned has gone off, and a word turned the same way comes out with its letters no longer in the order they were given.
What is missing has been taken out, so the letters named after this word are lifted away from the word standing before it.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder, taken exactly as they stand
a point is a peak, and lifting PEAK out of SPEAK leaves a single letter behind

annotation.walkthrough: 'Point' is a peak, and spotting that is the whole clue: four ordinary letters and one survivor, shuffled into the acronym Washington uses every day.
annotation.definitionFit: Premier -> POTUS: premier is used loosely for a country's chief executive, and POTUS is the acronym officials use for the one in the White House.

entries.clue: Date with Mr Bean from the telly outside saloon in US (5)

indicators.note: What stands outside a thing surrounds it, so the name just found closes around the letter clued beside it.

blocks.note: the Bean who is on television is the actor Sean Bean, and his first name opens after two letters
D is the standard abbreviation for date

annotation.walkthrough: Mr Bean pulls hard towards Rowan Atkinson. The Bean meant is Sean Bean, the Sheffield actor known here for Sharpe and Game of Thrones.
annotation.definitionFit: saloon in US -> SEDAN: what British drivers call a saloon car, with a fixed roof and a separate boot, Americans call a sedan.

entries.clue: Keep quiet pinching gold, alone in the Taj Mahal? (9)

indicators.note: Fingers pinching something close on it from both sides, so the word before this one shuts around everything that follows.

blocks.note: to keep mum is to say nothing, and the three letters open after the first
AU is the chemical symbol for gold
sole means alone, the only one there is

annotation.walkthrough: The definition is doing quiet work: the Taj Mahal is a tomb, built by Shah Jahan for his wife, which is why silence and solitude suit the surface so well.
annotation.definitionFit: the Taj Mahal -> MAUSOLEUM: definition by example, since the Taj Mahal is one grand tomb built to house a body, which is what the word names.

entries.clue: Call up the day before collecting permit (5)

indicators.note: To collect something is to gather it in and hold it, so the word before this one closes around the word after.

blocks.note: the eve of an event is the day before it, and the word opens after two letters
to OK something is to permit it

annotation.walkthrough: 'Call up' looks like a summons to the army, and the thing being summoned is a memory instead. Neither little word in the wordplay is doing anything unusual.
annotation.definitionFit: Call up -> EVOKE: to evoke a memory or a mood is to call it up, summoning something absent until it feels present again.

entries.clue: Freedom from restraint which Glastonbury stage might have? (7)

blocks.note: what a festival stage has standing on it is a band, article and all
a band that is playing is on, the word a festival uses for whoever is performing

annotation.walkthrough: Glastonbury is Britain's biggest summer music festival, held on a Somerset dairy farm, so the surface is entirely literal and the answer is a mood.
annotation.definitionFit: Freedom from restraint -> ABANDON: to dance with abandon is to dance without holding back, so the noun names the throwing off of self-control.

entries.clue: Sun now implying this rain? (7)

blocks.note: the calendar abbreviation for the day that follows Sunday's
if it is Sunday at this moment, the next day is not far off

annotation.walkthrough: 'Sun' reads as the thing in the sky right up to the moment you notice 'now'. It is a day of the week on a calendar, and the answer is a season of rains.
annotation.definitionFit: rain -> MONSOON: in South Asia the monsoon is the wind that brings months of torrential downpours, and the word is used for the rains themselves.

entries.clue: School nerd retaking sports (12)

indicators.note: To sport, in gardening, is to come up as a mutation unlike the parent plant, so what sports arrives in a form nobody planted.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a resit and a games afternoon. The answer is German for children's garden, borrowed whole into English for the youngest class.
annotation.definitionFit: School -> KINDERGARTEN: a kindergarten is the class small children attend before formal lessons begin, so it is a school by name and by function.
